blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: The characteristics of the equatorial and hot desert climates and why each behaves as it does, the tropical rainforest and hot desert ecosystems, and the causes and effects of deforestation.

blocks.heading: The equatorial climate
blocks.text: Places within about ten degrees of the Equator, such as Manaus in Brazil, share the equatorial climate. Every month is hot: average temperatures sit between about 26 and 28 degrees Celsius all year, so the annual temperature range is tiny, often under 3 degrees. Rainfall is heavy in every month, usually more than 2000 millimetres a year, and there is no dry season. The daily rhythm matters as much as the yearly totals: mornings are hot and sunny, and most afternoons bring a violent thunderstorm. The reason is the sun, which stands high in the sky at midday all year, so the ground heats strongly every day. Air heated at the surface rises, cools and condenses into tall storm clouds, giving convectional rainfall most afternoons. Humidity stays high because the forest and the rivers return moisture to the air. A climate graph shows this pattern at a glance, and reading one accurately is part of this topic.

blocks.heading: Reading a climate graph
blocks.text: On a climate graph the rainfall is drawn as bars, read against the left axis in millimetres, and the temperature as a line, read against the right axis in degrees Celsius. Two ranges are easy to mix up as well. The daily (diurnal) temperature range is the difference between the highest and the lowest temperature within one day; the annual temperature range is the difference between the warmest and the coldest month. At an equatorial station the daily range is often larger than the annual one, which surprises many learners: every day is hot, but no month is much hotter than another.

blocks.heading: The hot desert climate
blocks.text: Hot deserts, from the interior of the Sahara to the Namib coast, are defined by dryness: rainfall under 250 millimetres a year, often far less. Temperatures swing widely. Afternoons are scorching, in summer sometimes above 45 degrees Celsius, while the clear, dry nights can feel cold, so the daily temperature range is large, because dry air holds little moisture to soften the day's heat. The annual temperature range is large too, since winter months are warm rather than hot. Cloud is rare, so the sun burns through most days and humidity stays low.

blocks.heading: Why hot deserts are so dry
blocks.text: Desert dryness has three linked causes. First, around the tropics air sinks from high above and warms as it descends; sinking air does not form clouds, so high pressure dominates and rain rarely falls. Second, some deserts border cold ocean currents: the Benguela Current chills the air above the sea off Namibia, and cold air holds little moisture, so the onshore winds arrive dry. Third, deserts deep inside continents, like the central Sahara, lie too far from the sea for moist winds to reach them. Any one of these is usually enough to keep rainfall low; many deserts have two or all three.

blocks.heading: Ecosystems and the rainforest layers
blocks.text: An ecosystem is all the plants and animals of an area together with the soil, water and climate they depend on. The tropical rainforest ecosystem grows in layers: emergent trees break the sky above a dense canopy about thirty metres up, younger trees and shrubs stand below it, and the forest floor lies deep in shade. Only a sliver of the light reaches the floor, so few plants grow there until a fallen tree opens a gap. Dead leaves rot within weeks in the heat and damp, and the roots, often shallow and propped by buttresses, take the nutrients up at once, so the forest keeps its fertility in its vegetation rather than in its soil. A single hectare can hold more than two hundred tree species, which makes the rainforest richer in species than almost any other ecosystem on land.

blocks.heading: Drip tips and other rainforest adaptations
blocks.text: Rainforest plants compete for light, not water, and their adaptations show it. Drip tips are pointed leaf ends that channel heavy rain off the leaf, so it dries quickly instead of collecting water, growing fungus or being shaded. Buttress roots spread wide at the trunk's base to hold tall trees upright in the shallow soil. Lianas climb the trunks to reach the canopy light. A common error is to write that drip tips keep moisture in: in a forest that rains nearly every day, the difficulty is too much water, and the leaf sheds it.

blocks.heading: Desert plants and animals
blocks.text: Desert organisms manage scarce water in three main ways. Succulents such as cacti and euphorbias store water in fat stems and carry spines or small leaves, which cut the water lost to the dry air. Others grow roots that are long and deep or wide and shallow, catching water from brief showers before it evaporates. The welwitschia of the Namib, a living fossil with two ribbon-like leaves that can live for over a thousand years, drinks the coastal fog instead. Animals such as the oryx graze at dawn and dusk and rest in shade through the heat of the day, and many smaller desert creatures are nocturnal, emerging only once the air cools.

blocks.heading: Deforestation: from cause to effect
blocks.text: Deforestation is the large-scale clearing of forest. In the tropics the causes are commercial logging, cattle ranching, shifting cultivation and, increasingly, commercial crops such as soya and oil palm; the fruit of the oil palm gives palm oil, a vegetable oil, not a mineral oil pumped from the ground. Dams, mines and roads clear more forest directly. The chain of effects starts the moment the trees go. Without leaves to intercept it, rain strikes bare soil; without roots to bind it, the soil washes into rivers, so fields lose fertility and flooding downstream grows worse. The habitat is destroyed with the forest, and the people who lived in it lose their land. The effects then reach the whole planet: burning and rotting vegetation releases carbon dioxide, which adds to global warming, and species are lost for good. Local effects such as erosion, flooding and habitat loss are felt near the forest; global effects, carbon and biodiversity, belong to everyone.

blocks.heading: Brazil's clearing figures
blocks.text: Brazil monitors the Amazon by satellite and publishes the area cleared each year. The estimates show clearing falling steeply from about 28 000 square kilometres in 2004 to about 4 600 in 2012, after which the figures rose again, to about 13 000 in 2021. A trend answer names the whole journey, the fall and the renewed rise, not just the end points, and gives the years for each figure.
